opus-5.5.text:
I think generalization is probably the central question for agentic models right now, and it's harder than it looks.

When you train an agent with reinforcement learning, it's very easy to get a model that does extremely well on the environments you built. You construct a set of tasks, maybe coding tasks, search tasks, tool-use tasks, and the model learns to solve them. But the real question is: when it meets a new tool, a new website, a new codebase, or a task structure it has never seen, does it still behave sensibly? Often the honest answer is "partially." A lot of what looks like capability is actually overfitting to the distribution of environments.

So how do we think about it? A few points.

First, the base model matters enormously. Generalization in agentic tasks is largely inherited from pretraining. If the base model has a strong world model, good reasoning, and good long-context understanding, then RL is more like eliciting and sharpening abilities that already exist. If the base is weak, RL tends to teach narrow tricks. So we still believe very strongly in scaling the base model, and in improving token efficiency during pretraining, because that sets the ceiling for everything downstream.

Second, environment diversity is more important than environment difficulty. People naturally want to build very hard tasks, but if you only have a few kinds of environments, the model learns the shortcuts of those environments. What you want is a very large number of heterogeneous environments, with different tools, different feedback formats, different failure modes, so the only way for the model to do well everywhere is to learn something general: how to plan, how to read feedback, how to recover from errors, when to verify. In a sense, the environments themselves become a kind of data, and scaling them is like scaling data in pretraining.

Third, the reward design has to avoid rewarding hacks. Agents are very good at finding loopholes. If the verifier is weak, the model learns to satisfy the verifier rather than solve the task, and that behavior generalizes in the wrong direction. So a lot of the work is making rewards that reflect the real objective, and sometimes using models themselves to judge outcomes, with care.

Fourth, I think long-horizon behavior is where generalization really shows up. Short tasks can be memorized in some sense. But when a task needs dozens or hundreds of steps, the model has to keep a coherent goal, manage its own context, and adapt when things go wrong. Those meta-skills, like self-correction and reflection, seem to transfer across domains much better than domain knowledge does. When we see a model trained mostly on coding become better at research-style tasks, it's usually because of those meta-skills.

And finally, I'd say we don't fully understand it yet. There isn't a clean theory telling you which training environments produce which generalization. It's still quite empirical. You run experiments, you hold out whole categories of tasks, and you check whether improvement transfers. Our principle is basically: measure generalization on things you didn't train on, and be skeptical of gains that only appear in-distribution.

If I simplify it into one sentence: agentic generalization comes from a strong base model plus diverse, honest environments, and the goal is to teach the model how to learn and adapt inside a task, not just how to finish the tasks we gave it.

r001.rationale: The response calls generalization a central and difficult problem for agentic models, but it does not compare that challenge with training earlier dialogue models.

fable-5.1.text:
Generalization is really the central question for agents, and I think the honest answer is that we don't have it solved yet.

The way I see it, there are two kinds of generalization you have to worry about. The first is task-level: you train the model on some set of environments, and you want it to work on tasks it hasn't seen. The second is more subtle, which is generalization across the structure of the interaction itself. An agent operates over long horizons, it takes actions, it gets feedback from an environment, and the distribution of states it ends up in depends on its own earlier decisions. So the data distribution is not fixed. It shifts as the policy changes. That is a very different situation from pretraining, where the data is static and you just scale it.

The thing I've become more convinced of over time is that the bottleneck is not really the algorithm, it's the environment. If you train an agent on a narrow set of environments, you get a model that is very good at those environments and often quite brittle outside of them. The analogy to pretraining is useful here. Pretraining generalizes because the data is extremely diverse, and the model has to learn something close to the underlying structure of language and reasoning to fit it. For agents, you need something like the same thing: a large and diverse set of environments where the only way to do well across all of them is to learn genuinely general capabilities, like planning, verifying your own work, recovering from mistakes, and using tools in a compositional way.

So one way to say it is that we need to move from scaling data to scaling environments. And this is hard, because environments are expensive to build and expensive to run, and the reward signals are often noisy or hackable. Verifiable domains like code and math give you clean signals, and we've seen that reinforcement learning there transfers more than people expected. But a lot of real-world agentic work is not cleanly verifiable, so you have to think carefully about how to get reward signals that are good enough without being gameable.

The other thing I'd say is that long context and memory are part of generalization, not separate from it. An agent that can actually use its history, that remembers what it tried and why it failed, generalizes better, because it can adapt within a task rather than needing to have seen exactly that task before. In-context learning was a huge part of why language models generalized, and I think the agent equivalent is in-context adaptation over long interaction trajectories.

And finally, I think we should be a bit humble about measuring this. It's easy to get benchmarks that look great and then find the model falls apart on something slightly different. The real test is whether the model can do useful work in situations that nobody anticipated during training. That's a much higher bar, and I think it's the right one to aim for.

r001.rationale: The response calls agent generalization unsolved and contrasts agent interaction with static pretraining data, but it does not state that generalization is a greater challenge for agentic models than for earlier dialogue models.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what do we want the agent to generalize across? It could be new tasks, new tools, or new environments. Those are related, but they’re not the same problem. A model can perform well on new instructions while still struggling when the interface changes or when an action produces an unexpected result.

With agentic models, you also have this sequential aspect. The model takes an action, that action changes what it observes next, and a small mistake can move it into a situation it never encountered during training. So generalization is partly about choosing good actions, but it’s also about recovering—recognizing that something went wrong, gathering more information, and revising the plan.

My intuition is that we need diversity in the training environments, rather than just more examples within a fixed environment. We want the model to learn strategies that remain useful when the details change: how to explore, how to verify progress, and when to stop and reconsider an assumption.

And evaluation has to distinguish those things. If training and testing share the same underlying workflows, higher performance may reflect familiarity rather than a broadly useful capability. I’d want to hold out entire kinds of tasks or environments and see whether the model can adapt through interaction. That’s a much stronger test of whether we’re learning a general agent.

r001.rationale: The response describes challenges in agentic-model generalization, but it does not compare them with training earlier dialogue models or say they are a greater challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: what exactly do we want the agent to generalize across? It could be a new task, a new environment, a different set of tools, or simply a much longer sequence of actions. Those are related, but they’re not the same problem.

With agentic models, you’re also learning from the consequences of your own actions. A small mistake changes the state you encounter next, so errors can compound. A model might perform well on individual steps and still fail to complete the task.

So I would focus on both the diversity of the training environments and the way we evaluate. If you train on many tasks that share the same underlying workflow, you may just learn that workflow. You need to hold out meaningful variations—different tools, different task structures—and see whether the model can adapt.

The capability I’d really want is the ability to recover: recognize that an action didn’t work, gather more information, and change the plan. Generalization isn’t just producing the right plan on the first attempt. It’s being able to keep making progress when the situation differs from what you saw during training.

r001.rationale: The response discusses different dimensions and difficulties of generalization in agentic models, but it does not compare the challenge with training earlier dialogue models.
